opus-5.5.text:
Atmospheric rivers are a great example because they bring together almost everything that makes weather hard to model. They're long, narrow corridors of water vapor. They can be thousands of kilometers long but only a few hundred kilometers wide, and they carry enormous amounts of moisture from the tropics toward places like the West Coast of the US. When they make landfall, they can cause extreme rainfall, flooding, and landslides. So they matter a great deal for people's lives and for infrastructure.

From a modeling perspective, they're fundamentally multi-scale. You have a large-scale structure that develops over the ocean over many days. But what determines the impact is fine-scale detail: exactly where the river hits, how it interacts with the terrain, how the moisture gets lifted over mountains and turns into precipitation. If you only capture the coarse picture, you miss the part people actually care about. If you only look locally, you miss the global dynamics that steer the whole system.

That's exactly the problem neural operators are designed to address. A standard neural network on a fixed grid learns a mapping at one resolution. A neural operator learns a mapping between functions, so it captures the underlying continuous dynamics instead of the pixels. In something like the Fourier neural operator, global interactions are handled efficiently in the spectral domain, so you can model those long-range, coherent structures. And because you've learned the operator rather than a grid-specific map, you can evaluate it at different resolutions and zoom into the fine-scale behavior.

There's also the question of extremes. Atmospheric rivers sit in the tail of the distribution. They're the events that matter most and are hardest to predict. A model that does well on average but smooths everything out is not useful here. You need something that respects the physics well enough to produce sharp, realistic, high-impact events, and ideally to generate large ensembles cheaply so you can quantify the probability of those extremes.

So when I talk about what neural operators need to capture, atmospheric rivers are a natural illustration: global coherence, fine-scale local detail, physical consistency, and reliable behavior on the rare events. If you can get those right, you have a model that's useful for science and for decision-making, not just one that looks good on a benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response describes atmospheric rivers as thousands of kilometers long and says their large-scale dynamics require capturing global interactions and long-range coherent structures, explaining why non-local modeling matters.

fable-5.1.text:
Atmospheric rivers are a great example because they expose exactly what traditional grid-based approaches struggle with. These are these long, narrow bands of moisture in the atmosphere, sometimes thousands of kilometers long, that carry enormous amounts of water vapor. When they hit the West Coast, for instance, they can dump a huge fraction of California's annual rainfall in just a few events. So getting them right matters enormously for flood prediction and water management.

The challenge is that an atmospheric river is a multi-scale phenomenon. The overall structure spans continents, but the dynamics that determine where and how intensely it makes landfall happen at much finer scales. Small details in how the moisture plume interacts with coastal topography can be the difference between a manageable storm and catastrophic flooding. If you train a model on a coarse grid, you simply cannot resolve those fine features, and if you try to make the grid fine enough everywhere, the cost explodes.

That is the core motivation for neural operators. Instead of learning a mapping between fixed arrays of pixels, we learn a mapping between functions. The model learns the underlying operator that governs the physics, so it is not tied to any one resolution. You can train at one resolution and query at a finer one, and you can zoom into a region like the California coast when an atmospheric river is approaching. In our work with FourCastNet, we actually looked at how well the model captured these events, because they are a stress test for whether you have learned the right structure or just memorized smooth patterns.

The other thing I like about this example is that it shows why speed matters. Neural operators run tens of thousands of times faster than numerical weather models, so you can generate large ensembles and actually quantify uncertainty about where the river will make landfall. With a traditional model you might afford a handful of ensemble members. With a neural operator you can run thousands, and for a rare, high-impact event, that distribution over outcomes is what decision makers actually need.

r001.rationale: The response says atmospheric rivers span continents and have finer-scale landfall dynamics, but it does not explain that their large spatial extent makes non-local modeling necessary.

astra-6.text:
Atmospheric rivers are a good example because they connect very large-scale dynamics to very local consequences. You have this long band of moisture moving across the ocean, but where it makes landfall and how it interacts with the terrain can determine where you get intense rainfall or flooding. So you need to capture both the broad structure and the fine details.

That’s what we want neural operators to learn: how an entire field evolves, with interactions across spatial scales. It’s not enough to predict a reasonable average weather pattern. You need to preserve the structures that drive extreme events, and capture their location and intensity.

r001.rationale: The response describes atmospheric rivers as spanning the ocean and linking large-scale dynamics to local effects, then says neural operators must capture interactions across spatial scales. This communicates why modeling must account for spatially distant structure and local consequences.

sol-6.1.text:
Atmospheric rivers are a great example because they connect phenomena across very different scales. You have this long corridor of moisture traveling over the ocean, but when it reaches land and interacts with mountains, it can produce very localized, intense rainfall. So you need to capture both the large-scale transport and the fine-scale interactions that determine where that water actually falls.

For neural operators, that means learning more than a relationship between pixels on a fixed grid. We want to learn the underlying dynamics of the field, so we can represent those interactions across scales and work at different resolutions. And we need to capture the extremes, because getting the average weather right is not enough when the question is whether a particular location will flood.

r001.rationale: The response describes atmospheric rivers as long moisture corridors and says accurate modeling must capture large-scale transport alongside localized interactions. Its contrast with fixed-grid pixel relationships communicates the need to model effects across distant parts of the field.
